candidate.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity — use therapeutic communication, assess coping and support systems, and assist clients adapting to changes in health status
candidate.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — adjustment to a new chronic illness diagnosis
candidate.educational_objective: Support psychological adjustment to a new chronic illness diagnosis with validation, open-ended assessment, person-centered communication, and collaborative coping/self-management planning rather than imposing a fixed emotional-stage model.

options.A: Acknowledge the client’s feelings, use open-ended questions to identify specific concerns and supports, and collaborate on manageable next steps rather than assuming a fixed emotional stage.
options.B: Explain that every client progresses through the same predictable sequence of denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance before diabetes education can be effective.
options.C: Redirect the conversation to glucose targets because emotional reactions are not part of routine diabetes care.
options.D: Reassure the client that adjustment should be complete within a few weeks and that ongoing psychosocial support is usually unnecessary.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care recommend person-centered psychosocial care as part of routine diabetes management. Health care professionals should create a supportive environment for emotional disclosure, validate the individual’s experience, use open-ended questions and empathetic listening, assess available resources and barriers, and collaborate on coping and self-management goals. Current guidance does not require a universal stage-based adjustment sequence. B imposes a rigid model not supported as a required clinical pathway. C ignores psychosocial well-being, which is a critical component of diabetes care. D creates an unsupported timetable and may minimize persistent support needs.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Current diabetes standards support individualized, person-centered psychosocial assessment and emotional support during diagnosis and other changes rather than assuming that every client follows a fixed or time-limited adjustment sequence.
candidate.source_document_title: Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors and Well-being to Improve Health Outcomes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026; Comprehensive Medical Evaluation and Assessment of Comorbidities: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
candidate.source_locator: Section 5 Psychosocial Care, Recommendation 5.42 and accompanying text — psychosocial care is part of routine medical care; create supportive space for emotional disclosure, validate experiences, use open-ended questions and empathetic listening, collaborative goal setting and coping strategies. Section 4 Recommendations 4.1–4.2 — person-centered, strength-based, nonjudgmental communication and active listening
candidate.source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee
candidate.stem: A client recently diagnosed with diabetes says, “I feel overwhelmed and I’m not sure how this will fit into my life.” Which response by the nurse is best?
